I have four currently. I have only ever bought them directly from a dealer. I like to hold a Mosin before I buy them. I recently picked up an almost perfect 1945r M44 with bayonet from a dealer. Also, are you new to Mosins?

Yes I’m very new. I bought my first firearm in October and became addicted. I’ve been wanting to get my hands on a price of history and decided on a mosin to be my first antique pickup. I’ll take your advice and shop around at some local dealers. What should I be looking for in terms of quality that may not be obvious or apparent when holding one of these rifles?

Look for serial numbers, from the factory, on the stock, receiver, mag plate, and bolt. They should all match. That being said, quite often, the mag plates have two numbers. One will be scratched out and another will be placed next to it. Not a huge deal. This means that the rifle has probably been remanufactured, by the commies, in the past. Good or bad however you want to look at it.

Earlier usually means better quality. Pre-1940, the Soviets to time building the rifles and quality control was decent. When Germany invaded Russia, shit hit the fan and balls went to the wall. The Soviets pumped out Mosins as fast as humanly possible. As such some WWII Mosins have really shit quality metal work. The preWWII will be worth more, but they are worth spending $100 more. Speaking of which, if you find one at a dealer still wrapped in cosmoline and all the numbers match, BUY THAT SUCKER. You have a very high chance that no one fucked with the rifle.

I have a 1938r long barrel/M91-30 that has to be one of the best made Mosins I own. That being said, the stock and mag did not match. Great gun that I got cheap because it did not match.

Then you have the barrel length and ammo discussion. The longer non-carbine models have far less kick because of the longer barrel. 7.62x54r kicks like a mule in the carbine length. I have come across two common ammo varients; copper cased and steel cased. Copper cased has less powder and makes the carbine easier to shoot. Steel cased has somewhere around a 1/3 more powder behind the bullet. Not only will this kick the shit out of your shoulder, but you also have a higher chance of the casing jamming the bolt in the receiver with the carbine.

Jams are nothing to worry about though. The old Soviet manuals literally say to turn the rifle over and beat the bolt open with either your boot or a rock. It does work to be honest. I had a casing split about a hair width and jammed the bolt. My boot fixed the issue.

Just to help clarify terms; "Antique" is a very specific definition. It includes guns manufactured before 1898 and would usually be flintlocks, percussion caps, etc. and are specifically outside of ATF control and regulation.

The term you are looking for is "Curio and Relic" (C&R). These are guns that are at least 50 years old from the manufacturing date (and a few other definitions). That will include your Mosin Nagant.

While Antique firearms are basically unregulated, for your purposes buying a C&R firearm will be no different than buying any other gun. Collectors who will buy frequently can apply for a special C&R FFL license that allow them to act as their own FFL dealer.

I know you didn't actually mean "antique", but I wanted to clarify that since it carries very specific definitions and much different regulations.
